title: British Witchcraft Acts Repealed: End of Capital Prosecution in Britain
description: The Witchcraft Act of 1736 repealed both the English Act of 1604 and the Scottish Act of 1563, replacing capital punishment for witchcraft with a maximum penalty of one year's imprisonment for those 'pretending to exercise or use any kind of witchcraft, sorcery, inchantment, or conjuration.' The new framing treated witch-claiming as fraud rather than diabolical crime, an implicit declaration that witchcraft was not real. The repeal was associated with parliamentary debate that revealed a significant cultural divide: some saw continued belief in witchcraft as the position of the educated minority; evangelical religious opinion was divided. The same Vagrancy Act framework would be used against Spiritualist mediums in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
historiographical_note: Ian Bostridge's Witchcraft and Its Transformations c.1650–c.1750 (1997) analyzes the 1736 repeal in detail, showing that witch belief did not simply 'decline' as traditional historiography assumed but was transformed and contested. The parliamentary debate over repeal revealed that witch belief had become a marker of social and political identity, not merely a theological position. Owen Davies's work on post-1736 prosecutions under the Vagrancy Act shows that popular witch belief persisted well into the nineteenth century.
source_method: 9 George II c.5 (1736); Bostridge, Witchcraft and Its Transformations (1997); secondary scholarship
